prize_parts.citation: for the invention and precision realisation of optical lattice clocks, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: After reading all eight ballots I move my own first-place candidate, IceCube, to the alternative position and put optical lattice clocks first. The lattice clock is the one entry on which almost every member independently converges: it is first or second for four members and in every ballot. It also fits what I look for in a discovery, since nature is asked a quantitative question and answers it reproducibly. The magic-wavelength idea (Katori) removes the Stark-shift obstacle, and Ye's programme took the strontium clock to the 10^-18 level, with independent confirmation at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, SYRTE and NIST. The payoffs are concrete: a coming redefinition of the second, tests of constancy of fundamental constants and dark-sector couplings, and relativistic geodesy where gravitational redshift is measured across millimetres to centimetres. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. Seven of eight ballots independently name the same two people, and the contributions are separated into concept and demonstration without the usual overlap of theory strands.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a triumph of metrology and technique rather than a discovery that changes our picture of nature, and I have repeatedly argued that the committee should put discoveries before instruments. Frequency combs (2005) and ion-trap spectroscopy with Al+ clocks (2012, Wineland) already honoured the neighbouring lineage, so a third clock-related prize invites the charge of repetition, and the redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so the main payoff is still prospective. IceCube is the opposite case: a genuine new observational window, but with weaker attribution and source identification that is still only a few objects. I choose the clean, mature option, but I am aware that I am partly trading discovery value for attribution certainty.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first as a step in measurement capability, with independent confirmation from JILA, RIKEN, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, and notes the redefinition of the second is pending, so it is timely rather than late.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the two-name attribution. I would qualify the claim of a step in measurement capability as sufficient in itself. A factor of tens in accuracy is impressive, but the Nobel case rests on what it newly reveals. I will support the prize because the geodesy and fundamental-constant tests are genuine uses of nature as a probe, not simply because the numbers are smaller. I would want the citation to say the discovery is the lattice concept and its precision realisation, not the accuracy record, which will be overtaken.

responses.point: Lindroth argues the clocks are timely because the 2012 prize covered ion trapping and cavity QED and left clocks out, and that the magic-wavelength idea is simple and original.
responses.response: I accept the originality, but I disagree with the framing that 2012 left clocks out. Wineland's recognition was tied to manipulating single quantum systems, and his Al+ ion clocks are the same family, while Hall and Hansch in 2005 gave Ye's frequency-comb toolbox. The committee has to be able to say why this is distinct. My answer is that the neutral-atom ensemble in a magic lattice trades single-ion control for statistics and is a different concept, but the point needs an explicit statement in the citation, and I would not call the area unrecognised.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a new classification of electronic states, predicted by theory and realised in real materials, while accepting that omitting Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang is a fairness concern.
responses.response: I take the scientific point seriously, since theory confirmed by experiment is what I like. But the attribution problem is not a footnote. HgTe quantum-well experiments were done on the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, which the credited list excludes, and Mehlig notes that the 2016 prize on topological phases already covers the conceptual ground. I cannot support a fragile three-person split plus a prior-prize overlap when a cleaner candidate with seven names agreeing exists. I would keep B048 off my configuration.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, as the architecture under superconducting processors, a clean and mature piece of work with decades of confirmation.
responses.response: The science is excellent and I do not dispute maturity, but Mehlig himself points to the recent quantum-circuit recognition, and I think a second prize for superconducting circuits so soon after the last would be hard to defend. Wallraff's absence from the credited names is also a real attribution gap in the experimental first demonstration. Only three other ballots rank B008 at all, none above fifth, so I do not think the committee as a whole shares your ranking. I would hold it for a later year.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase entry first as a unifying geometric concept, arguing it is overdue and age is a practical consideration.
responses.response: I find the idea beautiful and the unifying role in molecular physics, polarisation and Hall conductance undeniable. My hesitation is priority: Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam and Mead-Truhlar make a two-name credit contestable, as you note yourself, and the effects were confirmed long ago, so the case is conceptual and historical. Only you and Lindroth (rank 5) have it ranked. I would not block it, but I want the committee to weigh it against a prize that has several independent first ranks.

responses.point: Pearce shares my first place for IceCube, weighing instrument-led discovery most heavily, with credit not clean because of the large collaboration.
responses.response: We agree on the science, and I take your reservation about attribution as my own. Since only the two of us rank it, I do not think I can push IceCube to the top without a stronger attribution argument, in particular on Spiering versus the DUMAND, AMANDA and collaboration leadership figures. I would keep it as my first alternative, and if you or the chair can find a clean way to credit it, I would reopen it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a third clock-related prize after 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (ion control, Wineland) as sufficiently distinct, and whether the redefinition of the second should be awaited.

Whether IceCube credit can be resolved cleanly beyond Halzen and Spiering, given DUMAND, AMANDA and collaboration leadership, which determines whether it should be paired with or replace the clock prize.
Whether a two-part prize combining a clean clock part with a single-name second part is possible without an arbitrary split.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My ties (Gross as former supervisor, Van Riet as co-author, the Uppsala string-theory group) do not touch these candidates, and I have no declared link to any named person. I am a string theorist and judge these experimental fields at some distance, which is why I rely on outside expert reports.
